extracted.intended_audience: members of the public and stakeholders participating in MSHA rulemaking (miners, mine operators, industry representatives, attorneys, and advocacy groups)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how MSHA conducts notice-and-comment rulemaking and what documents, analyses, timings, and contacts stakeholders should expect and rely on when participating in MSHA rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFR publication timing and access to copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 1 of Title 30 of the Code of Federal Regulations (30 CFR) is updated each July. All new rules that become effective between July 1 and the following June 30 are put in the next version of 30 CFR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New rules are often highlighted on the MSHA homepage where you can usually get a copy of the preamble and rule. You can also visit MSHA's Federal Register documents page. If you still need help and/or would like a copy of the rule sent to you by e-mail or regular mail, contact MSHA's Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances (OSRV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who to contact about rule questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions related to the enforcement of a rule should be directed to the Coal or Metal/Nonmetal Office, as appropriate. For questions about the history of a rulemaking, or a rule's background or intent, contact MSHA’s Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Agenda publication and content
rubrics_metrics.description: MSHA publishes a list of current regulatory projects in the Federal Register as part of the Federal government's Semi-Annual Regulatory Agenda (published around April/May and October/November).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Agenda describes workload for the next six months to a year and is divided into four sections based on the stage of the rulemaking: Pre-Rule, Proposed Rule, Final Rule, and Completed Actions. Obtain copies on MSHA’s website or at Regulations.gov.

rubrics_metrics.name: ANPRM vs NPRM (proposed rule) vs Final Rule vs Direct Final Rule vs Emergency Temporary Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and appropriate uses of different rulemaking document types: ANPRM, NPRM/Proposed Rule, Final Rule, Direct Final Rule, and Emergency Temporary Standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ANPRM: used when more information is needed or to solicit ideas/alternatives. NPRM/Proposed Rule: lays out planned approach, includes proposed regulatory text and preamble, requests comment; after publication and hearings the Agency may proceed to a final rule or re-propose. Final Rule: the enforceable standard/regulation published (regulatory text codified in 30 CFR; preamble not codified). Direct Final Rule: final rule without prior proposal when no significant adverse comments are expected; usually accompanied by a substantively-identical proposed rule; withdrawn if significant adverse comment is received. Emergency Temporary Standard: issued when danger is so grave immediate action is necessary; enforceable immediately while serving as a proposed rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble content and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A preamble is a discussion that provides detailed information about the background, purpose, justification, and technological feasibility of a proposed or final rule and precedes the regulatory text in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble for a proposed rule provides information about the reason for the rule and the alternatives the Agency is considering and asks the public to provide information, data, opinions, and concerns. The preamble for a final rule contains a discussion of the comments the Agency received concerning the proposed rule and describes how the Agency addresses these comments in the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between standard, regulation, and rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'standard' is promulgated under §101 of the Mine Act (30 U.S.C. 811) and includes MSHA health, safety, and training standards. A 'regulation' is promulgated under §508 of the Mine Act (30 U.S.C. 957) and includes MSHA approval requirements, petition for modification procedures, and civil penalty procedures. A 'rule' (per the APA) encompasses the development of a standard or regulation and can be used loosely to refer to either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authority under which a standard or regulation is promulgated is published at the end of the Table of Contents for each part (and for some subparts) of 30 CFR. MSHA can write an 'order' to close a mine for a violation of §104(d) or (e) of the Mine Act for standards, but not for regulations. MSHA can issue a 'citation' for violation of either a standard or a regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and administrative requirements that lengthen rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: MSHA (like other agencies) must comply with the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and other statutes and executive orders that require notice-and-comment procedures and various impact determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before publishing a proposed or final safety standard, the agency must determine the impact on the economy; on state, local, and tribal governments; on small businesses; on the health and safety of children; and on paperwork burden. For proposed and final health standards, the agency must assess the environmental effect. Department of Labor (DOL) and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) clearance requirements also add time. Final rules may still be subject to legal challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major procedural steps in promulgating a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary of the key tasks (22 steps) MSHA follows in promulgating a rule, with variations based on rule type (ANPRM, Direct Final Rule, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The steps include: Initiate regulatory action; Obtain an OMB determination of significance; Draft proposed rule, preamble, preliminary regulatory economic analysis, and information collection package; Clear regulatory action through MSHA and through DOL; Obtain Secretary of Labor approval; Obtain OMB clearance; Publish proposed rule in Federal Register; Transmit required information to SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy; Notify interested parties via email; Receive public comment; Hold hearings (if needed); Revise proposed rule and associated analyses to prepare final rule, preamble, and final regulatory economic analysis and information collection package; Clear regulatory action through MSHA and DOL; Obtain Secretary of Labor approval; Obtain OMB clearance; Obtain DOL and OMB clearance on information collection package and obtain paperwork burden control number; Publish final rule in Federal Register and place the final regulatory economic analysis on the agency’s website; Transmit required information to SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy; Transmit final rule to both Houses of Congress and the General Accounting Office; Notify interested parties of publication of final rule via email.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Economic Analysis (REA) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A REA is a document containing an analysis of the economic impacts of an MSHA rule on affected entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic impacts include both (1) the compliance costs (and cost savings, as appropriate) for segments of the mining industry covered by the rule and related industries (e.g., manufacturers of mining equipment), and (2) the related miner health and safety benefits. The REA is required by various executive orders and statutes (including Executive Order 12866, the Mine Act, the Regulatory Flexibility Act, and the Paperwork Reduction Act) and must address impacts and paperwork burden on the mining industry, other industries, and small mining businesses affected by the rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: PREA vs REA timing and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A Preliminary Regulatory Economic Analysis (PREA) accompanies a proposed rule, while a REA accompanies a final rule. For convenience, MSHA usually omits 'Final' and uses the acronym 'REA'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents of a PREA/REA
rubrics_metrics.description: A PREA/REA must contain specific analyses and determinations concerning the economic and other impacts of the rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required contents include: an overview of those segments of the mining industry affected by the MSHA rulemaking; a detailed discussion of the estimated health and/or safety benefits of the rule; a detailed account of the costs industry must incur to comply with the rule; a determination of the economic feasibility of the rule, as required under the Mine Act; a determination of whether the rule would have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities (per the Regulatory Flexibility Act and SBREFA); an estimate of the paperwork burden hours and costs imposed on the affected sector (per the Paperwork Reduction Act); and a determination of 'other' impacts as required by various statutes and executive orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and publication of PREA/REA
rubrics_metrics.description: The PREA/REA is not published in the Federal Register, but is posted on MSHA's website when the rule is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interested parties may view a hardcopy of the PREA/REA in the reading room next to MSHA's docket room or obtain a hardcopy from MSHA's Office of Standards, Regulations, and Variances. The published preamble contains a summary of the economic impacts as developed in the PREA or REA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether every MSHA rule has a PREA/REA
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all MSHA rules have a PREA/REA, but for 'small' MSHA rules with modest economic impacts, impacts may be estimated and described in the preamble rather than presented in a separate PREA/REA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commenting on a PREA
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone may make comments on a PREA during the regulatory comment period assigned to the rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no comment period for a REA, just as there is no specific comment period for a final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition for modification criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for modification requests to modify the requirements of an existing MSHA safety standard to achieve the purpose of the standard by different means. Title 30 CFR Part 44 sets forth MSHA's conditions for requesting a petition for modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MSHA will grant a petition for modification if the agency determines that the requested alternative provides miners at least the same level of protection as the existing standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variance definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: When MSHA grants a petition for modification, the petitioner receives a variance — the right to vary or do something different than what an existing MSHA safety standard requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variances are available only for safety standards, not health standards.
